scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Early Jersey Wakefield'

planting.note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost and transplant out 2–3 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop; in zone 8–9, also sow in fall (August–September) for a mild-winter crop, since the small, quick-maturing heads beat both spring heat and hard freezes.

directions: Set transplants 12–15 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the tight spacing and quick maturity make this variety well suited to succession planting and small-space gardens. Early Jersey Wakefield is one of the oldest cabbage varieties still in cultivation, introduced to American gardens from England in the 1840s and named for Wakefield, England, where it was developed. It forms small, dense, distinctively cone-shaped (pointed) heads of 2–3 pounds that mature earlier than nearly any other cabbage, historically prized for beating both the spring heat and cabbage-worm buildup that plague later varieties. The compact plants and short row-space needs make it a classic choice for small kitchen gardens, and its speed makes it valuable for a quick spring crop ahead of summer vegetables, or a fast fall crop in mild-winter climates. A true living heirloom with over 180 years of continuous garden use, in zone 3–9.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

planting.note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost and transplant out 2–3 weeks before the last frost; in the Gulf South, Charleston Wakefield is also a reliable fall-through-winter crop from a late-summer sowing, taking mild freezes without damage.

directions: Set transplants 15–18 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; keep evenly watered as heads size up to avoid splitting. Charleston Wakefield was selected in South Carolina from Early Jersey Wakefield stock as a slightly larger, slightly later-maturing improvement, retaining the same distinctive pointed, conical head shape while producing bigger 3–4 pound heads with a bit more heat tolerance for Southern spring gardens. It became a standard commercial and home-garden variety across the South in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, valued for uniform heads, good tip-burn resistance, and dependable performance under the variable spring weather of the Gulf Coast and Southeast. The sweet, tender, finely textured heads are excellent fresh, in slaw, or braised. A dependable regional heirloom for zone 4–10 gardens.

scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Late Flat Dutch'

planting.note: Start seed 12–16 weeks before the first fall frost for a fall/winter-maturing crop, or start in very early spring for a summer harvest in cooler climates; in zone 8–9, Late Flat Dutch is best grown as a fall-planted crop that matures through winter, since it tolerates hard freezes and stores in the garden far better than it handles summer heat.

directions: Set transplants 24–30 inches apart in deeply worked, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the large, heavy heads need ample room and rich soil to size up properly over their long season. Late Flat Dutch is a 19th-century American heirloom prized for producing enormous, flattened, blue-green heads that commonly reach 10–15 pounds and can grow considerably larger under good conditions, with dense, crisp interior leaves that make it an outstanding keeper — heads store for months in a root cellar or cool garage, and the variety was historically favored for large-batch sauerkraut and winter storage before refrigeration was common. Its long season and excellent cold hardiness make it best suited to fall planting in mild-winter climates like the Gulf South, where the heads mature slowly through the cool months and can stand in the garden through hard freezes without splitting. A workhorse heirloom for gardeners who want maximum storage cabbage from a single planting, in zone 3–9.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Glory of Enkhuizen'

planting.note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for a fall crop in mild-winter climates; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once seedlings have 4–5 true leaves.

directions: Set transplants 18–24 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the round, dense heads benefit from consistent moisture to avoid splitting as they finish sizing up. Glory of Enkhuizen is a classic Dutch heirloom cabbage introduced in the late 19th century from the seed-growing town of Enkhuizen in the Netherlands, long one of Europe's most important vegetable-seed production centers. It forms medium-large, round to slightly flattened, blue-green heads with a tender, sweet, finely grained interior that holds its quality well both fresh and cooked, and it has a good reputation for splitting resistance and reasonable storage life for a mid-season type. Widely grown across Europe and North America through the 20th century as a dependable, high-yielding main-crop cabbage, it remains a favorite heirloom for gardeners wanting classic round-head cabbage with proven, old-world reliability, in zone 3–9.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

planting.note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer/early fall for a fall crop; Shanghai pak choi bolts quickly in long, hot days, so in zone 8–9 it performs best as a fast fall-through-winter and very early spring green rather than a summer crop.

directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade; keep evenly watered, since any dry stress speeds bolting. Shanghai pak choi is a compact, fast-maturing bok choy type with pale jade-green, spoon-shaped petioles and glossy dark green leaves that form a tidy, vase-shaped rosette — smaller and quicker to mature than standard white-stemmed bok choy varieties, and prized for its exceptionally tender, mild, sweet stems that need no peeling or trimming before cooking. Its speed and compact size make it ideal for succession sowing every couple of weeks through the cool season, providing a steady supply of baby greens for stir-fries, soups, and quick braises. In warm-winter climates like the Gulf South it can be grown nearly through the whole cool season, from fall through early spring, before rising temperatures push it to bolt. Zone 2–10.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners
